utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom on this the second day of the first -- the first day of the second year of this trial. The Prosecution is represented by Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the Appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel and Muriel Cauvin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. On behalf of Kubura, it's Mr. Rod Dixon with Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and in particular our new usher who is assisting our Chamber for the first time. I'd also like to greet the court reporter and the interpreters, who are doing a good job. I have something I'd like to say about next week. A few days ago I said that because of the Plenary session that will be held on the 8th of December, on Wednesday, we will have to have a hearing in the afternoon on Thursday. That in fact, it would be possible to have a hearing in courtroom number II, in the morning on Thursday. So we can have a hearing on Thursday morning. The registrar will check this, but this is something I found out about yesterday afternoon. If there are no other issues to be raised, we could call the witness into the courtroom. But before we do so, let's go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could the usher call the witness into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to make sure that you can hear what I am saying, that you understand what I'm saying. You must be receiving the interpretation, unless you know French. If you can hear me and understand me, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a few minutes you will take the solemn declaration, but before you do so, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Samin Konjalic. I was born in Bosnia, in Travnik, on the 3rd of October, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you currently hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in Travnik municipality for the administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in what capacity do you work with them? Are you involved in administration? What are your exact duties in Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work as an official, or rather, as a professional advisor for the chief of the municipality, for the head of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind, and if so, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was a member of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. In a few minutes' time I will give the floor to Defence counsel who will examine you. But I would first like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed here. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel. You have certainly met them already. They are to your left. Usually their examination should take between an hour and an hour and a half. After they have completed their examination-in-chief - that's what we call it - you will have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. They are to your right. And they will conduct what we call their cross-examination. The questions put to you by the Prosecution have two objectives; firstly, to obtain clarifications to answers that you have provided to the Defence, and secondly to verify your credibility as a witness. These are the objectives of the cross-examination. The Prosecution is allocated the same amount of time as the Defence. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may re-examine you. The questions they put to you will be directly related to the questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination. When the parties examine you, you may be shown documents. You will then have a look at the documents and answer the questions. The three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time, but as a rule, the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to finish their examination and cross-examination before asking questions, because often the questions the Judges have might be questions that the parties will put to you. So we prefer to wait for the end. If we ask you questions, it may be to clarify some of your answers, or because we believe that there are certain gaps in your testimony. The Judges may also show you documents; we have a series of documents that are in the hands of the registrar. Once the Judges have asked their questions, and you have answered them, both parties may ask you additional questions. So you've probably understood that numerous questions will be put to you. If you feel that a question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it, because apart from the fact that we know you're a member of the civilian protection, the Judges know nothing about you. We don't have any written documents that concern you, and this is why your oral answers are so important. You should understand that your answers are very important for the Judges. Try to answer the questions as precisely as possible. This is what we expect of you. You are a witness, and a witness has certain rights and certain obligations. As far as your obligations are concerned, you have taken the solemn declaration. It is, therefore, your duty to speak the truth. However, if a witness gives false testimony, I should inform you of the fact that the witness could be prosecuted for contempt of court, and could be punished and sentenced to a term in prison. A witness has rights when questions are put to him. If you believe that your answer to a question might provide information that could be used to prosecute you at a subsequent date, in such a case, you may refuse to answer the question. This is the witness's right. But the Rules limit this right in that the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question. But if that occurs, the Trial Chamber grants the witness a form of immunity. This is a provision contained in our Rules, and it is a provision that exists to enable us to determine the truth. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of the hearing, do inform us of the fact. We are here to deal with any difficulties that may arise. I wanted to provide you with this information, as this is what we do whenever a witness appears before the Chamber. I will now give the floor to the Defence, who will provide you with additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Konjalic. As the President of the Trial Chamber has just said, I would also like to ask you to pay attention to one further matter; namely, the two of us speak the same language, and you would be able to answer my questions the moment I put it to you. However, both my questions and your answers need to be interpreted so that Your Honours and our colleagues in the courtroom could follow. Therefore, when I put my question to you, please wait a moment to give a chance to the interpreters to interpret fully, and only then answer it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Konjalic, where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I'm living in Bosnia, in a small town called Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you live at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I was living in the same country and in the same town, the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us what you are doing now. Tell us, what is your occupation and training, and where you acquired it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: By profession, I have a degree in politicology, and I graduated from the university in Sarajevo in 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service before the war, and if so, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did my military service in the former JNA, but I don't have a rank from that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your activities or duties until the beginning of the war, or just before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of the war, that is, up until 1990, I was working as a teacher of sociology in the secondary school centre. Before the war broke out, in fact, I transferred to the administration of the Travnik municipality, more specifically the civil defence, and that was the post I held when the war broke out. And throughout the duration of the war, I was in the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, could you tell us in greater detail what your duties were within the framework of the civil defence or the civil defence staff?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the staff at the beginning, and later I became chief of staff, and as of 1993, I was commander of the civil defence staff. I must also point out that after that I was also appointed commander of the district staff for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, which law governs the position and regulates the position of the civil defence in the country's defence.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The law on defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall, or do you know which forms of defence are stipulated by the law on defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: There's military defence and civil defence, according to the law on defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of defence was provided by the civil defence in which you held the positions you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Civil defence was part of the civil defence system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992 and 1993, which was the superior body above the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The superior body was the War Presidency, or rather, the government of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, what were the main tasks of the civil defence in those days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Not just then but then and after, the main duty of the civil defence is to protect the population and their property from any kind of man-made or natural disasters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to perform those duties, did the civil defence have certain resources so as to be able to protect and save people and their material belongings?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the civil defence applies the civil defence measures. There are several measures; if you wish, I can list them. And for each of those measures, there is a staff member in charge of that particular measure. So there are measures of rescuing, then finding shelter, measures against fires. There are 17 different measures that the civil defence resorts to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us which activities you were engaged in in the Travnik civil defence. Tell us, until when were you working in the civil defence, be it in the municipal or the district civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, throughout the war, you were working in the civil defence. Then you can certainly tell us whether the civil defence was a military or a civil entity.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The civil defence was a civilian entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was the civil defence at any point in time subordinated to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did, perhaps, units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they, perhaps, subordinated to civil defence staffs at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to my previous question, you said that you were subordinated to the War Presidency and the government. Tell me, which were the bodies that gave you assignments, instructions, and tasks which it was your duty to implement?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Our instructions came from the War Presidency, from the government, and, to some extent, from the operations group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were assigned tasks by units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were these tasks that you were obliged to carry out or were they just suggestions for you as a civilian body?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: A military body could not issue any orders to us; therefore, all their orders were more like suggestions as to what we should do at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in those days in 1993, what kind of relationship were you seeking to establish with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in your area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We were partners. We assisted one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the basis of your knowledge and experience from those days, did the civil defence encounter problems in carrying out its duties in Travnik municipality, and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I have to say that from the very beginning, as soon as the aggression against my state started, the civil defence premises were looted, though they were very well equipped previously. So they were left without the basic materiel and equipment. Because our warehouse was within the military facilities, there was one building where we kept our equipment. And when the aggression took place, there was a large influx of refugees to our town so that we were not ready for it, and none of the plans that we had made provision for any such thing. So we had problems providing food for the refugees, accommodating them, a shortage of living space, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some of the civil defence measures that you were able to undertake to protect and save people and property. Tell us, within the framework of the civil defence staff, were there people who were professionals? And to what extent were professionals important for the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: All members of the staff were professional people. Let me start with me as the commander. I completed my training and had all the necessary certificates even before the war, when I attended training in Belgrade, or rather, Zemun, for civil defence staff members. And most of my staff also had completed such training. These are mainly people belonging to the profession, so that the measure of protection against infectious diseases was led by an epidemiologist, a doctor, who specialised in this area. The measure for rescuing people from the rubble was headed by a graduate architect, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, in those days, who carried out civil defence tasks in the field, in villages, in local communes?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: There were local commune staffs that we trained, and also commissioners of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civil defence staff train the commissioners and local commune civil defence staffs?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were those commissioners in the field, and did they enjoy a certain degree of respect among the population?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Only a citizen of reputation and high ethics could become a commissioner for the civil defence, a person enjoying respect in his environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Konjalic, when you received reports from your commissioners or the commissions that you formed locally, tell us to what extent you felt that such reports reliable and accurate.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I never doubted the truthfulness of those reports, and I consider them absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your area there was a combat operation between the army and the HVO in June. Tell me, after those operations, did the civil defence staff receive certain specific assignments within the framework of its responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. We received such assignments both from the War Presidency and from the government and from the operations group, and what we had to do was to sanitise the terrain, and which is -- or, to clear up the terrain. And this is part of the activities of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, did the civil defence engage in other activities which were meant to protect abandoned property, agricultural land, and livestock?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is also one of our duties. We formed commissions which we sent out to the field to record the facts. And after that we sought to protect property, land, and everything else, such as livestock and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, answering one of my questions, you said that a large number of refugees had come to Travnik. Tell me, could you tell us roughly the number of refugees you're referring to when you say that they were numerous?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact figures, but I can tell you with certainty that, counting those that passed through Travnik and those that stayed in Travnik, there were more than 200.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the wartime situation, was it simple, was it easy to provide food and accommodation for such a large number of people?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Far from it. You see, Travnik is a town which had a population of 70.000 before the war, and it would happen that more than 30.000 people would reach our town in one day. So you can imagine the kind of problems we had to take care of those people, to feed them and put them up somewhere. These were superhuman efforts that my men had to invest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, are you aware that, after those operations in June, the majority of the Croat population from the Bila valley abandoned their homes and headed either towards Nova Bila or other areas under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. But I would add that the population moved not only from the Bila valley but from the town of Travnik as well, and all the surrounding villages. The Croats simply left their homes and went away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that such a large area was left without any population, in carrying out its duties of protecting property, was the civil defence confronted with additional and new problems?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Indeed, there were a large number of new problems that cropped up, the worst being, or the most important being, how to protect a large amount of property on such a large area, and with such few people that the civil defence had at its disposal and a small number of commissioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Konjalic, when, after these operations, the routes from Travnik towards the Bila valley and Zenica were opened again, did the population start to move again, and especially refugees who had been accommodated in collective lodgings?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was a stampede. These were large groups of refugees who were trying to save themselves in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, among other things, your task was to form commissions which were to organise moving into property that had been abandoned. Why did you believe that this measure would be a good one to protect property?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, the staff believed that if someone had moved into a house and lived there, it was easier to protect it. The person living there would protect it. This is what we tried to do. And in accordance with an order from the president and a member of the government, we tried to move a certain number of refugees into housing. Naturally, the appropriate procedure was followed when doing this. And, in fact, the houses into which people -- in which people lived were protected, so the staff was correct in making this assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my previous question, you said that there was practically a stampede of people, this large-scale movement of people. Did this have an effect on your work, or rather, was it impossible for you to carry out your task of moving people into these houses completely? And did you have to face problems such as these houses already being occupied by refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The civil protection, the civilian protection tried to move refugees into houses in a planned manner, but certain refugees preempted us and they moved into houses without the civilian protection being aware Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of this, without this being put on record. Naturally, they were concerned for themselves because they were bored with life in collective centres, and as soon as they could, they moved into abandoned houses. And this mostly concerned the houses nearer to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, when in the field, and when you made a record of the state of property and of the people moving into property, did you notice incidents such as looting or incidents involving the destruction of some of those homes that had been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you were not in the police, do you know to what extent it was possible, in the conditions that prevailed at the time, to determine who the perpetrators of these acts were? And did your commissioners tell you about when and how such acts were committed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, look, it was difficult to know who the perpetrators were, because most of these individuals were individuals whom the civilian protection did not know. Mostly, they were refugees; there were some local inhabitants, too, whose houses were destroyed or shelled. They remained without food, and you know that people were almost starving. So it was difficult to -- not to expect that someone might go into an abandoned house to take a bag of flour. People went to these abandoned houses in order to obtain a certain amount of food. This concerned a vast number of people, and the civilian protection -- no one from the civilian protection could say who was involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, this unfortunate process of stealing property or destroying property, did this take place throughout 1993 and later on, or was it over after a few days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it didn't come to an end after a few days. After a few days had passed, it was mostly food that was stolen. But the process continued. Equipment was looted, and even roofs -- roof tiles were taken, windows, doors, et cetera. So the looting of this abandoned property continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, did you continue to strengthen the measures that you had taken for protection, and did you re-examine the situation, the state of the property? Or rather, towards the end of 1993, did you take additional measures for the protection of the property and the livestock and the goods?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was our duty. And we continued to work to update our information and to continue to protect abandoned property, naturally, to the extent this was possible, because the commissioners and the members of the staff weren't able to be on duty around the clock. They couldn't guard every building in such a vast area throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said that you were a member of the civilian protection in the municipality or the district right up until 1995, could you say whether that problem, the problem of looting and destruction of property continued right up until 1995? Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher help us to show the witness a series of documents. I will then have a few questions to put to the witness in relation to these documents. We have a sufficient number of copies for the Trial Chamber and for our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, could you please have a look at document number 9, Defence number 1566. And once you have had a look at the first page, could you tell me whether this is a document from the civilian protection municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the last page of the report and tell me who signed it as commander of the civilian protection municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just have a brief look at the contents of the document, and once you have had a look at the document, would you stay that this is, in fact, what the civilian protection did in 1993, and are these the sort of problems that you had to confront at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. This would be the briefest sort of report compiled by the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 1 now. The number is DH1225. Mr. Konjalic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of duty did you perform in the civilian protection staff when Malenica Momcila was the commander?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph in this report, it mentions problems, or rather, the conclusions of your commissioners who had been in the field, and in line 1 it says that: "In spite of a ban prohibiting citizens to move around in the abandoned areas, a large number of citizens were observed removing abandoned property, taking away cattle," et cetera. What is stated here, would that be the result of your personal information and information that you obtained from your commissioners and municipal staffs?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. All the information and all the reports were compiled on the basis of reports from the field. For the staff to take a decision, it was necessary to have certain information either from the staff of a certain local commune or from commissioners from the area concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, you as chief of staff, and later on as a commander of the civilian protection staff, did you yourself go into the field and talk to your commissioners? Were you able to verify the claims that they made in their reports?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I must admit that this did not happen frequently, because, given my duties, I wasn't able to be absent from the staff very often. Whenever it was possible, I visited local commune staffs and commissioners in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at document number 2 now, DH1233. A while ago you said that you took various measures in order to protect and guard abandoned property. Would this be one of the ways in which you and the staff tried to protect abandoned property in a large area?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: If you like, I could provide you with an explanation of this certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, the civilian protection, when involved with the protection of abandoned property, took certain steps. They issued these certificates to individuals who were already in the village concerned. So if anyone else appeared and wanted to move into the abandoned house, or destroyed, in such a case, this individual could show the certificate obtained from the staff, this certificate demonstrating that this individual was responsible for the house or the property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 3, DH1256. Since you have mentioned the problems that you were confronted with, did you inform the government or the War Presidency in Travnik of these problems in good time, and did you request their assistance in dealing with the problems that you were confronted with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, and the person who signed it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document. It's from the civilian protection municipal staff, and I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a quick look at the document and tell me whether this is how you would inform your superiors of the problems and difficulties that you encountered when carrying out your tasks.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at document number 4, DH1302. Is this also a document you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also a document from the municipal civilian protection staff, and I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an example of how you would inform the government about the problems that you encountered when trying to move certain individuals into houses in an organised manner, in order to protect abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at document number 5 now, DH1303. A minute ago you said that people left collective centres, and there was a sort of stampede. But could you tell me if the collective centre, the collection centre, was a school or something like that, how many people were kept were kept there while the town was under blockade?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, for a certain period of time in the secondary school building, there was about four and a half thousand refugees. And in a room that was the size of a classroom in which you usually have 25 pupils, there were up to 90 refugees who slept there and lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a difficult situation, in fact, the reason for which they tried to move out of those buildings and, in a certain sense, solve this difficult problem?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were living in very difficult conditions. So whenever one attempted to do something new, this meant they were trying to improve their conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 5, DH1303. Does this reflect some of the problems you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to my previous questions, Mr. Konjalic, you said that you would receive tasks on a continuous basis, and that you carried out your duties and regularly informed the authorities of your problems. Please look now at document 6, 7, and 8, and tell me, please, whether you are familiar with this document, the document under number 6.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a document of your staff?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document of the civilian protection municipal staff, written by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it reflect a continuous concern about abandoned agricultural land in the municipality, and an attempt to let individuals use it provisionally so as to be able to survive and to protect that property at the same time? This document is Defence Exhibit 1537. Please look now at document number 7, Defence Exhibit 1540, and tell me, please, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also a document of the municipal staff which I signed as the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the problems of refugees, did you also have a problem regarding the provision of food and accommodation of displaced persons, and even the local population which was not receiving any kind of aid from international organisations, the UNHCR, and others that provided aid only for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Quite so. I have to state here that, during that period of time, the local residents were living under worse conditions than the refugees, except for accommodation, because the refugees would receive something, but the local population received nothing. They had spent all the food reserves they had, and we were unable to help them. So that the local residents were, in many cases, hungrier than the refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that situation why the abandoned land was being tilled, so that those inhabitants could be fed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Our aim was to allot land to the local inhabitants and the refugees for them to till so as to be able to grow food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at document number 8, please, and tell me, is it a document that you may be familiar with as an example of how you acted as the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. It is of the municipal civil defence staff, signed by the then chief, Mr. Irfan Samardzic, who acted as chief when I was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Defence document 1541. Mr. Konjalic, when you look back to the period in 1993, when you were performing such important civilian activities, could you tell us whether you did your very best under the prevailing conditions to protect the property of people who had left their homes, and, according to your sincere conviction, do you think you could have done anything more to prevent further devastation and destruction of that property?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We did everything that was in our power; I would say even twice as much. However, I wish to underline once again that when there was this stampede of people and all those developments, even had the civil defence been double in size, it couldn't have protected all the abandoned property, whether we're talking about houses, land, or livestock, because it's an enormous area, a large number of inhabitants, and a lot of houses and land. But we did everything we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did the civilian authorities call on the population that had left to come back, to return, so as to be in their homes, and also to protect all the damage that was inflicted on their property from the moment they left until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did everything to call the population to come back, but this was very difficult. You see, almost in all the villages there would be someone left, and it was easy in that case to protect them. But villages where there was not a single inhabitant, and a village is large, it was very hard to do anything, because, you see, you can't watch over a house 24 hours in order to save it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Konjalic, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the Defence counsel for the second accused got any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. My name is Daryl Mundis, and, along with my colleagues here, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have just a few questions for you today, sir, but I would like to reiterate what the Presiding Judge told you this morning in terms of the questions that I'll be asking you. And I would ask, if any of my questions are confusing or you don't understand them, please tell me that and I will rephrase the question. It is certainly not my intention in any way to confuse you by the questions that I ask you this morning. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You told us that there were more than 200.000 refugees in the Travnik area, or people who were passing through or remained in Travnik. Was that the total number of refugees, or were there 200.000 at any given point?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No. Never was there a total of 200.000. I said that more than 200.000 passed through Travnik, but the number of those who permanently resided in Travnik was between 25 and 30.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if you would, if you could turn to the document, that's tab number 3 that you have before you, which is DH1256. And if you look at the second paragraph, there is reference to "around 18.000 refugees." Do you see that in the document?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, sir, from this document, that at the -- or on or about the 25th of June, 1993, does that reflect the total number of -- or approximate number of refugees in Travnik municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: This was the number of refugees that the municipal staff knew the names of and their origin. But the number was much higher than this. These were registered refugees, registered in the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you also told us earlier that the civil defence or civilian protection staff was not in any way subordinated to the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us, though, that you did work together as partners with the army; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe it was your testimony that the army or its units would make suggestions to the civil defence staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I said that they would mostly suggest to us to do our part of the work; that is, they would signal when the time came, because of the war operations, for us to do our part of the work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned, I believe, twice this morning the operations group. I assume that that was the Bosanska Krajina operations group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that most of the suggestions that you received from the 3rd Corps came from the operations group, Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to the document, tab number 1, that you have in front of you, which is DH1255. I'd ask you, sir, to take a look at the first paragraph of that document, and you'll see in that document a reference to the orders of the OG Bosanska Krajina command. And I ask you if the use of the word "orders" is consistent with the notion that they were simply suggesting or working in partnership with the civilian defence staff, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, this word "order" was not interpreted by us as an order. This is the way in which an army operates. But for us, this was a suggestion, to act as suggested, to go along and carry out our measures. And those measures related to the protection of the livestock. And this was not an order issued by the government or the presidency, but it was more of a suggestion to the municipal staff for us to be able to start our work, because there were combat operations and we were not sure when it was safe enough for people to go out into the field to carry out their duties. So this was more of a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn now to some questions you were asked towards the end of the direct examination. You told us that many of the local residents were worse off than the refugees when it came to obtaining foodstuffs; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civilian defence staff have any interaction with humanitarian organisations to provide such food relief?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were working on a continuous basis with the humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this include foreign humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were in touch with the UNHCR, the International Red Cross, and Medicine Sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of foreign humanitarian workers in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: There were humanitarian workers who were foreign, not just in Mehurici but in the town of Travnik. Yes, there were some everywhere. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much liaison work --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not object to the previous question. The witness has answered it. But this question is not linked to the examination-in-chief, nor is it linked to the documents I have shown the witness. So I think we need to know on what grounds the Prosecution is asking this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you see there's an objection. But I note in document number 6 -- no, 5, I'm sorry, "Conclusion," under number 2, it says: "The government would ask Merhamet to continue with the operation." Isn't Merhamet a humanitarian organisation, a foreign one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a domestic humanitarian organisation, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could answer. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the organisation Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where that organisation is based?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of that organisation is in Sarajevo, and of the municipal Merhamet organisation, in Travnik itself. And it has branches, I think, in Turbe, Mehurici, perhaps in some other places, smaller branch offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, in order to fully respond to the objection to the prior line of questioning, I would ask that I be permitted to do so in the absence of the witness, unless the Chamber will permit me to continue asking a few questions along the lines I was pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us ask the witness to leave for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As the Trial Chamber is aware, there has been, on numerous occasions, evidence put before Your Honours about the foreign humanitarian workers in and around Travnik municipality, and especially around Mehurici. There has also been evidence before this Trial Chamber that such humanitarian workers came to Bosnia as humanitarian aid workers, but some of them subsequently took up arms under the guise of being Mujahedin. This witness has testified about the scope of his duties, which included, among the civil protection functions, of providing food, aid, and shelter to both the refugees and members of the local communities in the Travnik municipality. As such, and in light of his previous answer to the first question I put to him, this witness may be in a position to provide information concerning such foreign humanitarian workers. It's simply, Mr. President, it is a direct link to his testimony about the difficulties encountered by the civil protection authorities in terms of providing aid to the local community and to the refugee community. We believe that this is -- stems directly from his cross-examination, and we don't anticipate asking this witness a large number of questions on this issue. But it depends on what information, if any, he has that might be important to the Trial Chamber on this point. And, of course, the issue of foreign humanitarian workers and the links to the Mujahedin was set forth in the indictment as well, so we believe that this witness, because of the position he had, may have some relevant information that is of assistance to the Trial Chamber, and it's our position that that stems directly from his direct examination and the full scope of his duties during the time period relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor again to the Defence. But to summarise, the Prosecution tells us that they wish to put a question to the witness concerning humanitarian workers, whether they be foreign or national, and to ask him whether he knew that there were foreign humanitarian workers. And the Prosecution would like to be authorised to ask a question about the Mujahedin. The Prosecution tells us that, on a number of occasions, witnesses have come to testify about the presence of humanitarian -- foreign humanitarian workers who, at first, brought food, money, psychological support, and other kinds of support to the displaced population, and that subsequently these humanitarian workers were "converted" to armed combatants. And that is why the Prosecution would like to put questions to the witness. The Defence objected a moment ago, and in the light of what has been said, what is the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we fully acknowledge the arguments put forth by our learned colleagues from the Prosecution, that is, that they have a need to elucidate, investigate, or learn in some other way about the facts that my colleague has referred to and which have to do with foreigners, including foreign humanitarian workers, some of whom became men under arms. However, Mr. President, we are in a court, in criminal proceedings, and are strictly bound by the rules of this Tribunal. And Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, (H)(ii), the cross-examination is limited, and it is clearly stipulated what is allowed. And I will quote: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." So there are two convictions; that counsel shall put forth the nature of what they are trying to prove, and which must be in contradiction with the evidence given by the witness. So far we haven't heard any question that may be in contradiction with what this witness has said, so such a broad interpretation of the rights of cross-examination is not allowed in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and is in contradiction with the Statute of this Tribunal and the rights of the accused, especially as this witness has nothing to do with the Mujahedin or any other such broad issue which the Prosecution has offered in argument. So I think he cannot be said to have contradicted anything. And for that reason, we feel that the Prosecution should not be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. allowed to put such questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis, do you wish to respond to the Defence, whose arguments are based on the provisions of Rule 90(H)(ii), which says that when a party is cross-examining, he must show evidence that contradicts his testimony; and it must also specify the nature of the case which affects also the credibility of the witness. And there is point (iii) which refers to the rights of the Trial Chamber in that regard. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our position, actually, is that this would fall more under Rule 90(H)(i) because it arose out of subject matter of the evidence in chief, number one. Number two, however, let me put forward our position that, in order to get to the point where we can test the credibility of the witness, or put our case to the witness, we need to lay a foundation and establish if the witness even has any knowledge about the matter so that we can get to that point. And I would simply suggest that the first question that I put to the witness was getting to the point where we can determine if the witness does, in fact, know anything about these foreign humanitarian aid workers, not to mention whether we can then get to the next point that he may or may not know anything about, which is the issue of whether they, in fact, were converted, or some of them were converted, into Mujahedin. So I think it's actually a bit premature for my learned colleague to say that the witness doesn't know anything about the Mujahedin until I put those questions to him. If he says he doesn't know anything about them, then that's either the end of the cross-examination on that point, or I'm then going to challenge his credibility based on whether or not he could not know about that in light of the large amount of evidence on the point. So it's premature at this point to even be raising 90(H)(ii) until I've laid some kind of a foundation that would go down that path. But again, our primary response is that we are attempting to cross-examine him on matters arising directly out of his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is almost half past 10. We will withdraw and we will render our decision when we resume work, which will be at about five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will now render its decision relating to the objection raised by the Defence, the Defence's objection to the Prosecution's wish to ask the witness about foreign humanitarian workers in Travnik or in the area. Pursuant to Rule 90(H)(i), it was said that the Prosecution couldn't ask a question in its cross-examination that didn't directly relate to the answer of the witness. The Prosecution responded to this objection by saying that they could ask such questions, and all the more so in that the witness had answered a question about foreign humanitarian workers. The Trial Chamber believes that it is in the interests of justice for the witness, who was involved in the civilian protection, be asked about all the aspects of the work of the civilian protection, and this includes, naturally, the relations he might have had with humanitarian organisations, especially if they were in the area where he performed his duties. Therefore, the Prosecution is authorised to ask this witness the question. As a result, I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. The Prosecution may continue with its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, prior to the time when you were escorted out of the courtroom and we took the recess, I was asking you some questions about foreign humanitarian aid workers in Travnik municipality during the time period when you were with the civil protection. How much interaction, if any, did you have with the humanitarian aid workers, the foreign humanitarian aid workers, in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We did not communicate at all. I don't think I finished my answer, so if I may clarify what I said. I'm familiar with a humanitarian organisation called -- for children, it was called something like that. There were three organisations, Caritas, Dobrotvor, and Merhamet. And there was this organisation called Food For Children, that's what its name was. But I don't know whose organisation it is. I was informed that sometimes they would distribute milk or milk products for small children, for babies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, when you say "we did not communicate at all," did anyone in the Travnik municipal civil protection staff, or civil defence staff, did anyone in your staff have any communications with foreign humanitarian aid workers in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No. No. As far as I can remember, no. And it wasn't necessary. I don't even know how they distributed this food for children, and I don't know to whom they distributed this food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any requirement for such a foreign humanitarian organisation to register with the civil protection staff or the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know for how long the foreign humanitarian organisations were operating out of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to any of the foreigners who were working for humanitarian organisations in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you were familiar with them. Can you tell us how? In what way were you familiar with the work they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, this children's organisation, Food For Children organisation, was in the town itself. That's what it was called, although I don't know English. I knew that it was a humanitarian organisation that would provide or supply Food for Children and, on the whole, for small children. And as the UNHCR provided us with food for children, it wasn't necessary for us to have any contact with them or to work with them. I don't even know who were the members of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall how you became aware of their presence in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I saw this name, Food For Children, in the town. I asked someone what it meant, and a colleague of mine said it was an organisation that supplied food for children, and it was present in two or three locations. There was such an organisation in Mehurici, and I think there was another one in Turbe, which is in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Throughout your testimony today, it seems to me that the terms "civil protection" and "civil defence" have been used interchangeably. Is there a difference between civil defence and civil protection?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I don't know the exact translation. I don't know what civil protection and civil defence means in English. Civilian protection, "civilna zastita," means protecting people and people's property. Civil defence is probably a broader concept. It probably also involves a civilian power, civilian authorities, in addition to the protective aspect of the work. I'm still not sure what the right translation is, but I think that the term "civil defence" is perhaps more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That actually was my precise point. I wasn't sure the differences in the Bosnian language which perhaps contributed to the fact that it seems that the terms have been used interchangeably. So I guess my question really is: In Bosnian, the name of the organisation or agency that you worked for was "civil protection staff"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the correct term for the agency that you were with was the Travnik municipal civil protection staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any kind of agency or structure that was known as the civil defence staff in Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So references, then, in today's testimony to civil defence would, in fact, be to the Travnik municipal civil protection staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was referring to all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier you told us, I believe you testified that there was some training that you underwent to gain expertise in civil protection, and I believe you said you had that in Belgrade or perhaps an area near Belgrade; I believe you said Zemun.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, then, sir, that you had that experience or training prior to the war breaking out.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the civil protection staff believed that it was easier to protect civilian -- abandoned civilian real estate or property if there were persons living there in those abandoned houses; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that -- did that notion of the fact that it would be easier to protect property if persons were living in there, was that part of the training that you received to become a civil protection expert, manager?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's one way to assist the inhabitants, the population, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, was that the position of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government during the time period in question?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that that would be a principle that would apply throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was applied throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it was applied in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the principle involved would be applicable throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether it was applied or not, but the principle would remain the same.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's what we did. That's how we worked. If you like, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've done that previously. But let me just -- I'm curious about this, because it would seem to me that if that were a principle of general applicability, that the same principle would apply, for example, to abandoned Bosniak homes in the Krajina or in other areas where Serbs moved into those homes. Would that be -- would that fit within civil protection?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We applied this principle to Bosniak houses, too, not only in the case of Croat houses, because certain places were abandoned by Bosniaks, too, and we would move in two or three families there. And we would make them responsible for keeping watch over the other houses, and they were to inform us if something undesirable happens that we could then inform the competent authorities of the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, sir, a final question, if I could. The -- you told us earlier that the Croats in many areas in the Bila valley had simply left the area. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I do. They were taken away by the HVO. I have reliable information from Croat friends of mine who stayed on. They had very serious problems because they didn't want to leave. And afterwards, they weren't even considered to be good Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, because I told you that was my last question. I do have one more question. The documents that you've been shown today, the documents that you've been shown today that you had signed, you signed those with the title of commander, and the use of the term "commander" in the context of a civil protection service seems a bit alien to someone who maybe is not from Bosnia. I'm wondering if that was the regular term that was used for civil protection officers, and if that implied any other kind of function in terms of command, being the commander of the staff.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We'd been organised in accordance with the instructions issued. The civilian protection staff consists of a commander, a chief, and a certain number of staff members for providing protection. And what I signed wasn't just signed in a military capacity. We had staff sessions. And I must point out that my staff was multi-ethnic throughout the war; there were Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, and Albanians who were members of the staff; and there were even members of the Roma community. And after staff sessions, certain conclusions would be adopted. Only then can a commander sign certain documents, if information or an analysis is at stake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel? Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Konjalic, you mentioned the measures taken to move certain individuals into houses, or rather, to cooperate with the BH army, and you provided my learned colleague with a number of answers. Could you tell me whether this cooperation also involved taking measures to prevent property from being looted or damaged.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since this was the zone of responsibility of the Krajina OG, they'd have the responsibility or the authority to ban movement through that area. So we asked them that if individuals didn't have certificates that we had issued, that these people should not be allowed to enter those areas. This was to enable us to perform our duties more easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you now look back to that cooperation, could you tell me whether these bans, if they were bans, concerned areas where there was ongoing combat, or was it necessary for you to make any requests if you are performing your duties in the free territory?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, in the free territory, it wasn't necessary for them to give us certificates of any kind. On the whole, this took place in the zone of combat, where people's lives might be at risk. So we didn't know where the lines were, we didn't know where they were shooting from, so if a member of ours entered the area, his life might be at risk. That's why we asked the army to tell us where our people could go to perform their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, do you know whether the civilian and military authorities took any other measures for cooperation? For example, did they introduce a curfew, did they set up checkpoints to control the movement of the population, to the extent that that was possible, or were certain individuals arrested or prosecuted if it had been determined that they had looted or destroyed houses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a curfew for this very reason. At some point in time, in the evening, people who didn't have passes, permits, were not allowed to move around. The police was present in the town and they carried out their duties. They were involved in the security of the citizens in the town, and the troops were around the town where there was combat activity. And naturally there were checkpoints, too, because it wasn't that easy to gain access to the zone of combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned colleague asked you why the Croats had left that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to ask the witness my following question, could he be shown Exhibit P890.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, could you have a look at the document, please. In fact, this is a joint appeal to return to homes. When you were answering a question from my learned colleague, you said that you had personal knowledge from your Croat friends, that they said they were under great pressure to leave the area together with the HVO. Could you please tell me whether this document shows the sort of efforts made by the civilian and military authorities to ensure that all the citizens could return to their homes, in order to protect their own property, among other things, because the MUP and army forces were not able to secure all of the houses.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's just what I said. This is the first time I've seen the document, but I'm familiar with its contents, because to Muhamed Curic, the president of the War Presidency, I made such a suggestion. And I'm glad that they did in fact draft such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were such appeals forwarded to citizens through the media and in other ways so that your citizens could return and move back into their houses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. We proceeded in this manner all the time. The civil protection did this, too, as well as certain Croats who had remained in the town; they would appeal to their family members to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague also asked you a question that concerned certain principles, was it a principle that was followed, was one of the principles the idea that the abandoned houses should be occupied, was there a decision, a conclusion, from the War Presidency and the government on the basis of which you took action in certain situations.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't have acted in any other way. We received from the government, or rather, from the War Presidency an order, according to which we were do everything we could in order to protect property and goods, and we acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, do you know whether, in the course of the war, many series of life were governed by decree laws issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at assemblies of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can remember this, perhaps not. But do you know whether, in 1992, a decree law was issued on temporarily abandoned property, and was there another decree on temporarily abandoned flats? And did these decrees regulate how abandoned flats and abandoned property was to be moved into? And did these decrees guarantee that people who had left such property could return.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was familiar with that, and not just I. All the staff members were familiar with those decrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In accordance with those laws, at the end of the war, and when those people returned, was this property returned to those people in accordance with the law? And when they had suffered damage, were they compensated?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the cases where civil protection moved people into property legally, a record was made of the property found there. And when the owner returned, the individuals in the houses had to return the property, the house, and the items used. And these items were included in a list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question concerns the titles "commander" and "chief" of the civil protection staff. You said that you were a civilian body, and I'm interested in that name, because my colleague said that this might confuse someone who is not from Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I would like to know is whether these names have anything in common with the name of the commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence and the chief of staff of the Territorial Defence, or rather, does it have anything in common with the name of the command of some military unit, or the command or chief of some military unit? Are the bodies in question completely different, or is something else at stake?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: These bodies are completely different. The commander of the civil protection, the chief of civil protection, these are names that have absolutely nothing to do with military formations. This was our system of command and control in the case of the units of civil protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Konjalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have a certain number of questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try from the beginning to clarify this question of the status of your entity, called the civil protection staff, in relation to the military. Would you be kind enough to look at the documents which the Defence has shown you, and specifically document number 1. When you look at document number 1, to the left, on the top - are you reading like I am - is there a registration number and a date and a subject? Yes? You, who did your military service in the JNA, this format of a document, doesn't it have a military aspect to it? Because we could show you military documents which have exactly the same format. What would be your explanation?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: This is the way in which offices functioned; the protocol number, the date, and this was obligatory in office work, in administrative work. After that the document is archived under this number so that you can find it whenever you need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So this is just a pure coincidence that the form of this correspondence coincides with military correspondence, but you're telling us that it is administrative. Is it also coincidence that you had the title of commander of a staff? Is that also an administrative matter, to be commander of a staff?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't an administrative title, it was a title, it was a rank, it was a function. We had our ranks, too. If they hadn't stolen our uniforms, you would see what rank the commander of the civil protection had; we had insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have answered a question I was going to put to you. I was going to ask you whether you had uniforms, and you just told us that they stole your uniforms. So you had a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With insignia and a cap?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you possibly armed.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: According to the Geneva Conventions, a civil protection cannot bear arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you did have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: We had a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. To resolve a problem of translation in English, will you please look at document number 1 and document number 2, because the English translation of your institution, once it is called civil defence and the second time as civil protection. So I want to find the identical word in your language. There are two different translations into English. Document 1 and document 2, do they come from your institution?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
