utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I wish to draw the attention of the Defence, because they are producing the documents, that this prompted some questions from the Prosecution, you must have noted that the English translation sometimes is civil defence and sometimes protection, but the witness tells us that it is one and the same entity. So in the documents, and my questions are based solely on the documents, I have noted that in the documents provided to us that you also had the responsibility of collecting bodies, the bodies of persons killed in the area of operations. And please look at document number 3. Was it your duty to take care of corpses and to bury them, because there's reference to burial here, too.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a civil protection measure. We call it sanitation. And the aim is to prevent infectious diseases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In concrete terms, how did this happen? When the army certainly was able to call on you to collect the bodies and to bury them, how did this happen, to the best of your recollection? Who would call you? What were the logistics that you had to do this? What did you do to identify the bodies? Because in your report, which is to be found within the file provided by the Defence, and it is document number 9, in which you refer to the burial of 70 people who were killed, 50 identified and 20 not identified. To make it clear to the Judges, could you tell us how this happened; how were you warned, how you went out into the field, and what you did there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: You see, when there are combat operations, one army forces the other to move. And when the army pushes back the enemy forces, it's normal to expect that there will be dead on our side, because then it is territory liberated by our army. We know because we can hear the shooting. You can hear the cannon and the shells, and we're all ready to act; a unit is ready, with stretchers and everything else that is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small question stemming from what you have just said. You say, "We were prepared." Were you aware of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the military operation taking place before it took place? You say that you were preparing yourselves. If you were, it meant that you knew what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you obviously have not understood me. The town of Travnik is in a valley with two mountains, on one side Vlasic and on the other Vilenica. And when a bullet is shot 5 kilometres away, you can hear it, not to mention a shell. But that was a military secret. How could we know about military operation? But our units, not just this one for sanitation, but also the fire brigades and everything else, was ready to act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would hear shells and bullets. How could you deduce from that that there were dead if you were 5 kilometres away? Somebody must call you to tell you to collect the bodies. Who? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was mostly somebody from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did so by telephone, or how did you communicate with the army? Was it by telephone? Did they come to see you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I told you that in the field we would had commissioners. A soldier would reach the closest commissioner in the area and he would tell him what was happening. And then the commissioner, through his couriers, would inform the small staff in his local commune, and that small staff was duty-bound to inform the staff of which I was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Now, to collect the bodies, what did you do? Did you have vehicles to transport them? And what did you do to identify them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: These were vehicles, not special vehicles, but the vehicles we had. And we would go out into the field and collect the people killed, the bodies of the people killed. The identification was done by the competent body, and that is the MUP or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were the bodies taken?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That depended. Sometimes they were buried on the spot, if these were local residents, and if somebody recognised them and wanted them to be buried there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would bury them in the cemetery of the commune or on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No. They would mostly be buried at the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And suppose that you don't know who the dead person is. What happens?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Then the police, using certain methods that I'm not familiar with would write down as unidentified persons, NN, and then we would get the green light, if the person had been registered under a certain number as an NN, and we would get the signal from them when we could bury that person once they had all the information they needed about it, about the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were the one to bury the bodies, who placed the bodies into the ground.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you did this, was there a death certificate and a permission for burial? Did you have a death certificate allowing you to bury the person, or was it done just like that, without any documents?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: All the persons had the necessary documents. Not a single person was buried just like that, without being identified, marked. If a family member was there, it would be done in the religious manner, the way they wished, and where they wished the body to be buried. The body would be transported to that spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to another subject, and that is the occupation of abandoned buildings into which you would house refugees. In the documents provided by the Defence, I have noticed that sometimes they have refugee cards. So these 200.000 refugees, or 18.000 at a particular point in time, these refugees, did they all have ID cards testifying to the fact that they were refugees? How did you do that? Would you, indeed, check these cards to make sure that they were refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every refugee living and staying in Travnik municipality had a refugee card with a number and the basic information about him; where he came from, when he arrived, and how many members he had in his household, so the members of his household were listed on the card, too. And the refugees in transit would stay for a day, or two on the outside, and then they would head off to Zenica or to some foreign countries. And those refugees were just registered on paper but they were not issued refugee cards, because they did not wish to reside in Travnik, so they were in transit. We took them over, we put them up, provided food for two or three days. Some people did not stay longer than two hours. They had relatives in Zenica and they would go on to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the refugees who stayed, you said that they had to be accommodated, and vacant flats had to be found for them. What did you do to establish that there were vacant apartments? Did you have employees under you who went around the streets to make a record of abandoned apartments?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The Travnik municipality had a commission that made a list of abandoned apartments, and the civil defence -- civil protection had lists of households from their commissioners. So we knew how many households every village had, or how many houses there were in every village. We even knew the owners of those houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you're telling us that the municipality would prepare a list of abandoned apartments, and you were given that list. To the best of your knowledge, the persons who abandoned their houses, and when leaving they didn't know that refugees would come to replace them, to the best of your knowledge, did the municipality requisition those apartments for occupation? Because the Penal Code of your country has a provision that protects private property, so private property is protected and one cannot appropriate it. And to put someone in there in the place of the legitimate owner, there must be a document requisitioning that apartment. So was there any such thing, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not familiar with the term "requisition."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a document coming from the municipal authorities saying that a particular apartment or house was being temporarily placed at the disposal of the refugee? Was there that type of document? You're saying yes.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such documents which were issued for temporary occupation of an apartment, and it stated "until the return of the rightful tenant"; and that they were duty-bound to look after it and to restore it to their rightful owners in the same condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you're still in charge of all this area, to the best of your knowledge, in the years that followed, was there any litigation over the occupation of these apartments? Were there owners who found that something had been stolen, that their property had been damaged? Are you aware of any lawsuits afterwards with regard to these apartments? And did they inform you of the looting of abandoned houses? People left, locked the door, and when they returned nothing was left. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that the Travnik municipality is the first municipality that received the certificate of an open city. It is the first municipality to which refugees have started to return. We have an acknowledgement of that. And also, we were among the first to restore property, so that in Travnik municipality, there are no outstanding issues regarding the restoration of tenancy rights or property. There are cases when something was taken away from an apartment; the furniture may be missing, all of it. But each tenant or holder of tenancy rights, as he has a document from the municipality showing what his belongings were, he may seek, through the court, compensation for those goods. Now, whether there are any cases in court, and how many, I'm really unable to say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to another subject. A minute ago you said in response to a question put to you that there were humanitarian organisations present, and you mentioned a number of them. But if I've understood you correctly, you had no contact of any kind with these humanitarian organisations. Isn't that paradoxical, given that you're a member of the civil protection? You were waiting for aid that might arrive from charitable organisations, and yet you say that you had no contact with them. Could you elaborate on your answer, which I find very confusing.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the Merhamet, Caritas, and Dobrotvor organisations, the humanitarian organisations that belonged to three different ethnic groups, the town was under blockade and those humanitarian organisations were to take care of their people. But given the blockade of the town, they did not have any food supplies. They couldn't help them. The UNHCR and the International Red Cross had instructed us to distribute the food that we received to refugees and displaced persons alone, and we were to provide them with lists of these people. They controlled the goods we distributed on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer presents two problems. You said that there were three humanitarian organisations, Merhamet, Caritas, and Dobrotvor. And according to the English translation, you said that they took care of certain ethnic groups. Could you tell us which ethnic groups they took care of.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Merhamet took care of the Bosniaks; Caritas is a humanitarian organisation for the Croats, for Catholics; and Dobrotvor was a humanitarian organisation for Serbs, for those of the Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have now clarified that matter. And the second problem that arises is that you said that you would act in accordance with the instructions issued by the refugee committee or the International Red Cross. Were you completely dependent on these two international organisations? Could you explain this us and provide us with some examples? Because this is the first time we have heard of this.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The UNHCR had its rules and standards, and this organisation obtained the greatest amount of food for refugees and displaced persons. After food was distributed in Travnik, and given the number of refugees, the UNHCR stated how much food should be distributed to one person. And on the basis of these criteria, we provided food for, for example, a family that consisted of four members. We compiled these lists, and it was our duty to return these lists to the UNHCR. It was on the basis of these lists that they would come to check on a daily basis whether the people concerned had received the goods as stated in the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as the Red Cross is concerned, what sort of relations did you have with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, they operated in a slightly different way. It was easier for us. The International Red Cross had parcels for various individuals, so it was easier for us to distribute them. We didn't have to weigh the food, pour drinks into containers, et cetera. So, for example, a family of five members would receive five parcels of that kind. And our cooperation with the International Red Cross was very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that the other Judges have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as commander of the civil protection staff, how many employees did you have under you, more or less?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps about 700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you receive daily reports on what happened in your -- or what was happening in your region, reports that came from members of the civil protection?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the whole, if it was possible to send such reports from the field, I would receive them. This was the case if there was no combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Croats left their houses, you would agree with me that there was looting and that property was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You agree with that. Members of the civil protection staff, did they provide you with reports on this looting, on incidents of theft? Would you receive such reports from civilian protection staff?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they forwarded reports stating that property was being looted on a large scale. This involved a lot of people. A lot of people entered these abandoned houses and looted the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So were they actually able to see the people who were involved in this looting?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they mention the names of these individuals in the reports that they forwarded to you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they mention the names of the people who were involved in the looting in their reports?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't mention their names because they didn't know who these people were. They didn't know them. There were people who had come from all over the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So since you had these reports, what did you do? What steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, at the same time we would move people into abandoned houses, and we tried to save whatever could be saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you contact the police to conduct an investigation, either the civilian or the military police? Didn't you inform the police?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the police was already present in the field. Early in the morning the police went out into the field, both the civilian and the military police. They tried to take steps to prevent these incidents. And civilians were banned from moving around that zone, so the army and the police had issued such orders. Strangers were not allowed to move around those abandoned areas, apart from members of the civil protection. However, the police and the army cannot block or cut off an entire village and prevent anyone from entering or leaving. So if a stampede of 500 individuals enter one village, well, you can imagine what members of the civil protection or three policemen could do in such a case. It was very difficult to witness such events. I saw a woman who was 60 years old and she was carry 25 kilos of flour; she could barely walk. The woman was basically hungry. And even if they had tried to take that flour, that bag of flour from her, well, it would have been very difficult to do that, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that the police were already present in the area. Did they arrest the individuals who were involved in looting? Was any follow-on action taken? Were the police investigations followed up?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The police had blocked all the entries. The dirt roads and the asphalt roads to the villages had been blocked. There were police checkpoints, and people would be checked when entering or leaving. But these people would find new routes of access. You know, in Bosnia, there are people who are still coming in and going out. We can't prevent this. And how could the civil protection or five policemen prevent someone from entering a village? It was very difficult. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a house was in an isolated area and only members of the civilian protection had seen the individuals involved in looting, if the police wasn't aware, you were aware of the fact because you had seen their report. If we imagine such a case, what would you do? You wouldn't contact the police? If the police wasn't aware of the fact and you were the only body aware of what had happened, what would you do in such a case?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened in one village, in fact. But by the time the police had reached the village from the checkpoint, there was no one left in the village. The people had fled through the forest, with their food. They didn't find them there. So when the police returned to the checkpoint, they probably returned, these looters probably returned to the village. Looting occurred especially at night, when it wasn't possible to see anyone. They could pass through checkpoints without being noticed, et cetera. So it was during the night that this occurred most frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question that relates to a question that was just put to you. It appears that you yourself witnessed an incident. You mentioned a woman who was carrying a bag of flour, a sack of flour. So can you confirm this: You ourselves actually witnessed a looting incident, and if so, where was it, where did this take place, and do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, on that day I had set off to see my parents, and they in fact lived there. As I was driving by, I saw this very old woman who was carrying a sack of flour. I couldn't really say whether it was her sack of flour, but I saw that and I just wanted to mention this example because it's a very sad scene, when you see an old woman carrying such a sack of flour because she just wants to survive, she doesn't want to starve to death. I found that very sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. To pursue the discussion on the activities to prevent them, to repress looting, you said this morning also about resettling new persons in abandoned houses. This was a measure to protect the houses. These new inhabitants could keep a watch on the village, "and they would report to us and we could then inform the competent authorities." That's a quote from page 40 of the transcript. I think I know what you meant by using the expression "competent authorities," but could you tell us for the record what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole I was referring to the police. We had the phone number of the police and we would contact them and inform them that, at that point in time, in such and such a place, looting was going on. Civilian protection members were women; they couldn't prevent this, they couldn't get involved in a dispute, and they couldn't take away the goods that had been stolen. So on each occasion, the police would go into the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And if, in this context, you talk about the police, you're talking about the civilian police, I suppose? Or have there also been cases in which you provided the information to the military police, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: As far as securing buildings is concerned, as far as securing property is concerned, it wasn't our duty to inform the military police. They were responsible for something else. It was the civilian police's duty to protect the civilian population, and to protect me as the commander of the civil protection as well as my property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: A few weeks ago we had a colleague from your organisation, Mustafa Hokic here in the courtroom. I suppose you know him. You do?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When he was aware, we got different reports from the civil protection staff, among them some reports on the destruction and burning of houses in the municipality of Travnik. And it struck me that there was an attempt made in some of these reports to reconstruct the causes of a housing having burned down. If there were indications that this might have been a criminal act, would you send such a report to the civilian police or to other authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. That was our task. We had to inform the civilian police about what had happened in the field, and that was the task of the commissioners. They were to monitor everything and inform them what had happened, especially if anything unusual had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two questions on the reports relating to the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have two questions on the documents that have been shown to you this morning. I'm sorry. Again, I have two questions to put to you on the documents that were shown to you this morning. The first one is the document number 4, and it has the number 1302. I would like to ask you a question on the second linea, second sentence of that linea. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: "Apart from a property inventory record, none of the people housed were issued a temporary housing decision, because this staff is not competent to issue such a decision." What you told us this morning seemed to imply that there were competent to take decisions on housing people in abandoned houses. This might contradict what you said, so I'm just asking for some clarification, how I should understand this phrase. Could you give me an answer?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The civil protection, through its commissioners and lower level staffs, would move certain persons into a certain house, make a report about the owner of the house, and make an inventory list, as well as the auxiliary buildings, and all the other information would be taken from the people moving in. And their duty was to make a report about this move, and all these things had to be inserted. The report had to be in three copies; one was given to the person who was moved into the house to live there, one went to the civil protection staff, and a third was given to the government so that the competent authority for housing should issue a decision on the temporary occupation of that apartment, because that was the only body that had the authority to issue such certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is on the document that has the number 1566, the third page. There is a Roman IV on the third page on the "Evacuation and Sheltering of Endangered and Suffering Population," and in the second linea, you mention almost 28.000 individuals being sheltered in the area of Travnik; some 2.000 were accommodated in collective centres and some 25.000 in private homes. Now, you talked before about private homes, abandoned private homes being used to find a place for displaced persons. Could you give an estimate of how many of these 25 or so private homes were abandoned houses just to give us an idea of the quantity of the phenomena?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: A certain number of refugees were put up in private homes, but a certain number of them found accommodation with relatives; another group had the resources to rent places; then some stayed with friends. So the figure regarding collective centres were living in conditions that were really not deemed for man. The rest of the refugees moved into these abandoned homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it's hard to say; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: It is very hard, because, you know, these are living beings and the numbers change. And it is very difficult to have such figures. People were coming and going all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: A related question I had, but perhaps that also is impossible to answer, is how many houses, abandoned houses in the area where the fighting was in June 1993, Guca Gora, et cetera, all these places in the community of Travnik, how many houses, abandoned houses, would be used to resettle people in that period? Can you give us an estimate? Was it systematic? Was it sporadic? Tell me anything you know about it.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: It was many years ago. I knew the figures by heart if you were to ask me in the middle of the night, but I find it very awkward to give you a figure now in court. But anyway, every house that had the minimum conditions for living, if it just had a roof - only those without roofs or windows were not moved into - the rest were. And also the houses that were far from the city, because refugees didn't wish to travel a lot, they wanted to be close to town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So as a rule, they were used to resettle people. I'm aware of those exceptions. Is that a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My last question is about the humanitarian organisations. You mentioned three different organisations, one Bosnian, one Croat, and one Serb. The Merhamet organisation, was that a local organisation or a foreign organisation, or a mixture of both? That is a question that has been put to you but we haven't yet heard an answer on it.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Merhamet was founded in Sarajevo, and that is where its headquarters are, in the captain of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it has its branch offices, one of which is in Travnik. I think they're called municipal boards. The composition of Merhamet, that is, the composition of the managers, are exclusively Bosniaks. But the beneficiaries are not only Bosniaks. Canteens that they organised were used by Bosniaks and Croats and Serbs and Romanies and Albanians and the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The word "Merhamet," is that a Bosnian word or an Arabic word? And what does it mean, by the way?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I don't know Arabic, but Merhamet means aid, in my view, aid to those in need. Because when we say of somebody that he is Merhametli, it means that he's a person who wants to be helpful, kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still on this issue of the Merhamet. If I understand you correctly, the term "Merhamet" is a Bosniak term; in your language, it means charitable or kind? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: My mother, when I was 7 years old, said to me, Son, you must be Merhametli, and my understanding of it was that I should be a good man, help others, and that is why I take special satisfaction that in this war I was Merhametli, I helped people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Merhamet organisation that had a branch office in Travnik, what was its address? Do you know the address of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: It was close by, in the center of town. It had its offices in two or three places, because they were probably doing something, cooking and the like. But I can tell you that as I'm now working in Travnik municipality, I want 5 marks to be deducted from my salary every month as membership fees for Merhamet, because there are still people in Travnik who are short of food. So I am glad to renounce 5 marks a month to feed someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, my understanding was that you had no contact with them. Are you confirming that you had no contact with them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that I didn't have any contact with them, because there was no need. I was doing something quite different. I had a great deal of things to do, and I couldn't take care of the residents as well. That would be too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the light of what you just said, will you look at document number 9, please, page 4.10. It's a document that you signed. And paragraph 10, I will translate into French what it says in English: "Organising humanitarian and other actions in the municipality." And I'm still translating. "The civil protection municipal staff initiated and launched a series of humanitarian actions." And I continue on page 5, again, from your pen you say: "In cooperation with the Basbunar --" What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: It is the public utility enterprise, responsible for cleaning the town and providing the population with water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Under chapter 11, headed "Cooperation," could you read what you wrote about cooperation. Read it out in your own language, this paragraph, the first paragraph under the heading "Cooperation."

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: "In order to carry out planned activities and tasks, the civil protection municipal staff of Travnik cooperated closely with international humanitarian organisations, local organisations, competent state organs, and military unit commands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isn't there a contradiction there between the question I put to you a moment ago when you said, "I never saw any of the Merhamet people; we had no communication."? And here you say that you cooperated fully with all the humanitarian organisations. How can you explain that contradiction between what is written here and what you just told us? For anyone reading, and that is why I asked you to read it, gets the impression that, according to this paragraph, you were fully cooperating with international organisations, the Red Cross, et cetera, but also with local humanitarian organisations, so certainly the three, Caritas, Dobrotvor and Merhamet. Is there a contradiction, or is this a printing error? Because I'm trying to understand what you're saying from the point of view of credibility, but I see a contradiction there.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I am sorry that you appear to have a poor translation. It says "organisations in the municipality," not "humanitarian." It may be a mistranslation. There are many organisations; there are work organisations and so on. It doesn't say "humanitarian organisations" here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read once again in your own language the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. "In order to carry out planned activities and tasks, the civil protection municipal staff of Travnik cooperated closely with international and local humanitarian organisations, competent state organs, and military unit commands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your own language, there's obvious mention of humanitarian organisations, both international and local. The purpose of my question was to see whether there were links between civilian protection in Travnik and the Merhamet humanitarian organisation, and you said no, because you did not meet with them. Is that what you're still confirming? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I can't deny that. I can't say that I never met and saw these people from all these organisations. And when speaking about humanitarian organisations, I wish to speak about all three and not just Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you're telling us that you did meet with them. So if you met with them, what was the name of the person in charge of Merhamet? It must have been somebody of some importance.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I do know. His name was Mustafa Indjic. I do know that. And for Caritas, it was Don Pavo, and Dobrotvor, I think his name was Djoko, or something like that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These humanitarian organisations which, as you told us, provided food and certain consumer goods, to the best of your knowledge, where did their finances come from? Have you any idea of who financed them, how they were financed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know who financed them at the time. I said a moment ago that, just now, I am a member of Merhamet and I am paying a membership fee. But I know many friends of mine who are also members of Caritas and Dobrotvor, et cetera. These are humanitarian organisations whose task is to assist. I never inquired into the business policies of Merhamet or any of the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a final question which comes to mind just now, following what you've just said. The food they gave, did they buy it on the spot or was it coming from the outside? The food, was it being brought in from outside or was it purchased on the spot, from local peasants? To the best of your knowledge, where did the food come from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I think there may have been both, but I'm not sure. I do know that in my village, the village I was born in, they did purchase a certain amount of potatoes from the peasants. Now, whether there was some from outside, I'm not sure. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when they were buying these goods, was it paid in German marks, in local currency, in American dollars? Do you know how they paid for this?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I think they issued coupons. We had coupons. We didn't have a currency at first, we just had coupons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they paid for what they purchased with coupons.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That was the means of payment, not just for Merhamet. I would buy cigarettes with coupons too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 12.30. We're going to have our technical break now, and we will resume at about five to 1.00. I will give the floor to the Prosecution for any questions stemming from the Judges' questions, and of course I will give the floor to the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions that arose out of the Judges questions to you. The first one concerns the notion of, I believe as you put it, sanitising the battlefield, that is, collecting the bodies following any combat or any other type of action. I would like to ask you, sir, if at any point around the 9th of June, 1993, the Travnik municipal civil protection staff was involved in any way in collecting bodies from the area around Milena and Bikosi.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember such an event. If the terrain was being cleaned up, then my men were probably involved in the operation. There was no one else to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, then, in light of that answer, to the best of your recollection, during the period, say, June 1993, were units of the ABiH ever involved in clearing up the battlefield or clearing up an area where combat or fighting had taken place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: It was the civilian protection alone that cleared up the terrain and removed the dead bodies and the dead animals. Our purpose was to ensure that no infectious diseases spread. Our purpose was to prevent epidemics of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, in response to a question from one of the Judges, you told us that Travnik was the first, I think you used the term, "free city," and the first place where refugees started to return -- yes, people who left had began to return. Were you referring, sir, to Croats, Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not just to Croats, to Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your recollection, sir, when did those Croats and Serbs begin returning to Travnik, municipality, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I think that they started returning immediately after the Washington agreement had been signed, after the cessation of hostilities, in other words. And we have, from the international community, a certificate on being an open town. It's recognition for -- a form of recognition for everything we did to ensure that people could return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you can, can you give us an approximate number of Croats and Serbs who returned to Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't provide you with any numbers right now, but in terms of percentages, about 70 per cent of Croats, or perhaps even 80 per cent of Croats, returned. Maybe about 50 per cent of the Serbs returned. Everyone could return, but unfortunately some people went to Scandinavia, to parts of the world across the ocean, and they probably won't return. On the whole it was the elderly and those who had no where else to go who returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, you responded, again to a question from one of the Judges, that some of the refugees, and now, sir, I'm talking about Bosniak refugees who came from other parts of Bosnia into Travnik municipality, you said that some of those refugees had the resources to rent houses. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be a little more specific in terms of who those people rented the houses from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various cases. People from Krajina who had been wealthy, they managed to bring some money from them. But since the accommodation provided in collective centres wasn't very nice, they decided to use the money to rent a flat or a house. In some cases, they would rent accommodation from Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. It depended on who was letting such a flat. On the whole it was Bosniaks who let flats. In some cases, a Bosniak would send his family out of the town and remain alone. And if that Bosniak had a big flat, he might decide to let two rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any instances where the Bosniak refugees were renting flats or renting property from the Croats who left?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Of course there were such cases, many such cases. They would rent houses, too. Before the Croats left, there were quite a few Bosniaks who lived in Croatian houses. And when the Croats left, they remained, the Bosniaks remained in those houses. My commissioners in the field, when they came to see who had moved in, they saw that these people had valid papers that had been given to them by the owners of the houses, papers stating that they had the right to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of cases where the Croats who had abandoned their property were renting -- basically what I'm saying is that the Croats who left, were those houses then put into the rental market?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: They weren't rented, they were moved into. Who would have rented them? They weren't let. Who would have let them? In certain cases, if there were two brothers and one left and the other remained, in such a case, the brother who had remained would let the house belonging to the brother who had left. There were such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence counsel. Further re-examination by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back to some of the questions that the Chamber put to you. You were asked about your cooperation with international humanitarian organisations. In order to be quite clear, could you tell me, who was the civil protection was responsible for as far as providing them with accommodation and food?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: They were responsible for refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have already spoken about the difficult situation that the local population was in, and this can be seen in some of your documents, too, tell me who the local humanitarian organisations cared for on the whole. You mentioned three organisations, Merhamet, Caritas, and Dobrotvor.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took care of the local population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the different categories of people that you and the local humanitarian organisations took care of, was that the reason for which your contact with the local humanitarian organisations were not as frequent as the contact you had with international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the main reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these three local humanitarian organisations that you have mentioned, could you tell me whether there was a local municipal committee of the Red Cross in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a local municipal Red Cross committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Jewish organisation, a Jewish humanitarian organisation, the name of which was La Benavolencija?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I couldn't answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, although you have already spoken about this in response to a question put to you by the Chamber, in the case of Merhamet, Caritas, Dobrotvor, and the Red Cross, in the case of these local organisations, who were the people who were their members? Were the staff of these operations local inhabitants or were they foreigners, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in all three humanitarian organisations, the leadership consisted of people from Travnik alone. They weren't from the wide area; they came from the town of Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber was interested in the meaning of the word "Merhamet." Could you tell us whether Merhamet is originally a Turkish word, or is it a word the origins of which are different?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I would say that Merhamet would sooner be a Turkish word rather than an Arab word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know the exact meaning of this word, but you said that you knew the meaning such as it was used -- the meaning of the word such as it was used by your mother. Tell me, is Caritas a local word or is it derived from some other foreign language?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that Caritas is derived from the Latin language, although I don't speak Latin, I don't know Latin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the word "Caritas" the word that our people usually use, and do the people know what the meaning of this word is?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what the meaning of the word is, but I don't believe that most of the citizens know what Caritas means, although they have heard this word. They know that Caritas is a voluntary humanitarian organisation, but as to the actual meaning of the word "Caritas," to be quite frank, I myself am not quite sure of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to help the Trial Chamber, could you tell us whether Dobrotvor and Crveni Krst, the Red Cross, are local Slav words, and everyone knows the meaning of these words?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you help the Trial Chamber with regard to certain linguistic difficulties. Given the historical development of our language, would you say that there are many foreign words, words that come from the Turkish language, from the German language, from Romance languages, and this depended on the period during which we were occupied by Turks -- the Turks, the Austrians, the Italians, et cetera. In other words, that come from these languages which have become local words, and we all know what the meaning of these words are although we can't translate them.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there are certain words of that kind that we use every day, on a daily basis, in spite of the fact that we might not know the meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you help us to understand something else. I asked you whether in the Serbian language there are many words that come from the Arab -- the Arab language and the Turkish language. Would you say that Serbs also use such foreign words?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Serbs use just as many foreign words of that kind as the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we speak about organisations such as Merhamet and Caritas, we believe that these are local words, the meaning of which is familiar to us, and we don't find it strange to see that certain organisations have such names.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and especially since these organisations are humanitarian organisations, so the translation of these terms would have something to do with humanitarian affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now show the witness DH29, Defence Exhibit DH29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, we have a newspaper here, and this is a decree law on defence that you have referred to, and this law regulates the responsibilities of the civilian protection as well. Is this the decree law that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber asked you about the structure of those units and about the names used, so could we have a look at Article 50 in this decree law. And could you read out paragraph 2 in this article. Have you found Article 50?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Article 50, paragraph 2: "In the units of the civilian protection staff, there should be no individuals serving in the armed forces; workers of the MUP, and policemen; pregnant women and single parents who have children who are under two years of age, or two children over ten; members of KP Doms; and people who are not fit to serve in civilian protection."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of this decree law, can we see that members of the civilian protection staff or civilian protection units couldn't be members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Konjalic, is it quite clear from what you have read out that you, in fact, had nothing to do with the organisation of military defence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at page 10 in this decree law, and under number 4. Could you read out the titles that you have there. There's Roman number IV, and then we have the numbers 1 and 2. The article concerned is Article 62.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Article 62.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you read the title above the article, the heading? What does this regulate?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: "The civilian activity and the organisation of military defence, joint provisions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above Article 64?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: "The armed forces."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this part, is there a reference made at any point to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at the title under number 5.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's above Article 70.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: "The civilian activity and the organisation of the civilian defence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether this is part of the defence within the civilian sector? And you said that civilian protection was part of this, too.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read out Article 71.

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: "Within the framework of civilian defence, the following elements should be organised and developed: Civilian protection as a system of protection and a system for saving; monitoring service and an intelligence service; encryptographic measures, apart from the needs of commanding armed forces; planning training apart from members of the armed forces; and protection of companies and other legal entities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the title after that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: The title that follows is "Civilian Protection."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the entire text that follows explain all the tasks and the measures and the way in which the civilian protection operated, the civilian protection force that you were in in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This is a section that refers to the civilian protection of which I was a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Article 71, we also have the service of observation and information. Tell me, is that also a component part of civil defence and a component part of the civilian organs of authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a component part of civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This service of observation and information, did it have round-the-clock duty, and did it collect information about everything that might be of significance for the civil defence as a whole?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had duty round the clock throughout the duration of the aggression, from the beginning of the war until the end of the war. And even today, this service of observation and information is still active, because of various reports of fires and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your numerous tasks that Their Honours have asked you about regarding the clearing up of the terrain, and your reaction when you learnt of looting and burning of buildings, this service for observation and information, was it the first competent body which should have informed you that something was happening in a certain area that the civil protection had to react to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: They did so usually with the help of sirens, and we knew exactly when there was the beginning of danger from the air, the end of such danger, or any other disaster, such as a fire. So we could tell which it was on the basis of the different sirens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the civilian defence, did you cooperate directly with this observation and information service?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the framework of that, did you act in accordance with your resources and assignments?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question is linked to the question put to you by Her Honour, when you informed the civilian police that there was looting of property, as a citizen of Travnik, Do you know that the perpetrators of crimes who were discovered, whose identity was established, were they processed, prosecuted, and sentenced?

utterances.speaker: SAMIN KONJALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are quite a number of them that have been processed. Some of them were reported by the civil protection and some other bodies. Now, what the outcome of those trials was, whether they were sentenced or not, I don't know. Some of them may be ongoing. But if it was possible, without any doubt, to establish somebody's identity and the crime he committed, reports were filed against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions arising from the questions Your Honours posed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, your hearing has been completed. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish to thank you for coming to The Hague to testify. You have answered all the questions put to you both by the Defence and the Prosecution, and the Judges. We wish you a safe journey home, and we hope you will continue your activities in the civilian protection with success. Could the usher be kind enough to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has four documents to tender, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We would like to tender into exhibit 1537, 1540, 1541, and 1566, as these are documents which the witness himself compiled or signed, and documents he was aware of in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have four numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are admitted under the following numbers: DH1537, English version 1537/E; DH1540, the English version DH1540/E; DH1541, English version 1541/E; and finally, DH1566, and the English version 1566/E. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We take note of those exhibit numbers. In the few minutes remaining, I would like to make a correction linked to a translation problem. In the oral ruling that we rendered on the question of new documents, I wish to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that the French version, on page 12524, lines 5 to 9, and the English version of this paragraph is page 15524, lines 22, 23, 24, and 25. In the English version there is an error in relation to the French version. In French, the following was stated, and I read: "Stemming from this principle, the Prosecution cannot produce within the framework of its cross-examination of a Defence witness new exhibits which have not already been admitted with a view to strengthening the Prosecution case, or to introduce new elements regarding the criminal responsibility of the accused." So this paragraph clearly indicates that the Prosecution cannot produce new documents during the cross-examination of a Defence witness. And in the English version, beginning with line 22, in English it says: [In English] "As a result of this principle the Prosecution can only present in the course of its cross-examination of a witness ..." [Interpretation] So that in the translation, it says "can" rather than "cannot," so obviously "cannot" should have been said. So I wish to draw the attention of the Prosecution to this point so that they take note of this correction. From time to time there are errors. We discover them subsequently, and when we discover them, we let you know. But you, too, may discover some. So I wanted to tell you this so that there should be no ambiguity. As you know, we have a witness for tomorrow afternoon, and next week we will be continuing with our sittings, as indicated yesterday and this morning. Are there any other points to be raised? If not -- Mr. Dixon is telling me "no" with his head. I see that there are no other matters to address. I thank you. And please be back here tomorrow for the sitting that will begin at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of December, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
